subject: physics
question_text: Define the two principal specific heats of a gas. Which one is greater, and why?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 (Thermodynamics) Short Answer Question 2 (printed p.126). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: c_P = (1/m)(ΔQ/ΔT) at constant P and c_V = (1/m)(ΔQ/ΔT) at constant V are the per-unit-mass specific heats; c_P > c_V because constant-pressure heating also does external work while constant-volume heating does not; the molar relation C_P − C_V = R holds for the MOLAR specific heats (per mole), giving c_P − c_V = R/M for the per-unit-mass forms defined in this card, where M is the molar mass.

steps.label: Specific heat at constant pressure
lines: The specific heat at constant
pressure, c_P, is the heat needed to
raise the temperature of unit mass
of a gas by one degree, at constant
pressure.
steps.margin_note: Say UNIT MASS and CONSTANT PRESSURE — both words are needed for the definition.
steps.why: The word 'unit mass' is what makes this the specific heat and not the molar specific heat — the two are different quantities with different units.
common_mistakes: Leaving out 'constant pressure' — without it the definition does not distinguish c_P from c_V.
Writing the definition for one mole instead of unit mass — that is the MOLAR specific heat, a different quantity.
steps.memory_tip: c (lower case) is per unit MASS; C (upper case) is per MOLE — different quantities.

steps.label: Specific heat at constant volume
lines: The specific heat at constant
volume, c_V, is the heat needed to
raise the temperature of unit mass
of a gas by one degree, at constant
volume.
steps.margin_note: State it the same way as c_P, but with volume held constant instead of pressure.
steps.why: c_V is defined exactly like c_P, with the one condition swapped — comparing the two definitions side by side is what the next mark is built on.
common_mistakes: Copying the c_P definition and forgetting to change 'pressure' to 'volume'.
Saying c_V applies only to a gas in a sealed container — it is a property of the gas, defined under the condition of constant volume.
steps.memory_tip: c_V holds Volume fixed; c_P holds Pressure fixed — match the letter to the condition.

steps.label: Why c_P is greater
lines: c_P is greater than c_V.
At constant volume no work is
done, so all the heat raises the
internal energy alone.
At constant pressure the gas also
expands and does external work,
so more heat is needed for the
same rise in temperature.
steps.margin_note: Give the REASON — work done at constant pressure — not just the fact that c_P is bigger.
steps.why: Both specific heats raise the temperature by the same one degree; the extra heat in c_P is spent doing work, not raising the temperature further.
common_mistakes: Stating c_P > c_V without giving the reason. The reason is the mark, not the fact alone.
Saying temperature rises more at constant pressure. The rise is the same one degree in both; it is the heat needed that differs.
steps.memory_tip: Constant pressure heat pays for work too, so it always costs more than constant volume heat.

steps.label: The molar relation
lines: The molar specific heats C_P and
C_V (heat per MOLE, not per unit
mass) obey a similar rule: C_P is
larger than C_V for the same
reason.
For one mole, C_P − C_V = R (R the
universal gas constant); the
per-mass forms used above satisfy
steps.margin_note: Say the MOLAR relation uses R, and the per-mass relation above uses R divided by M.
steps.why: c_P and C_P are different quantities with different units, so the same-looking rule (bigger minus smaller equals a gas constant) takes a different constant in each case — R for molar, R/M for per-mass.
common_mistakes: Writing c_P − c_V = R without the /M. That relation holds only for the MOLAR specific heats.
Mixing lower-case c and upper-case C in the same line — they are different quantities and must not be interchanged.
steps.memory_tip: Molar minus molar gives R; per-mass minus per-mass gives R divided by M.

insider_note: c_P and c_V here are per unit MASS, not per mole — do not write c_P − c_V = R without the /M for these.
